screen.title: Announcement: Fire drill
screen.prompt: Listen to an announcement in a residence hall.

audio.text: Good morning, residents of Hall B. A fire drill is scheduled for tomorrow at ten a.m. When the alarm sounds, please leave by the nearest stairway, and do not use the elevators. Gather on the lawn across the street and wait until a staff member tells you it's safe to return. The drill should take about fifteen minutes. Thank you for your cooperation.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the announcement?
options: To report a fire in Hall B
To prepare residents for a safety exercise
To announce repairs to the elevators
To invite residents to an event on the lawn

why.en: Purpose (paraphrase of "fire drill"). A takes "fire" literally; D misuses "lawn".
why.tr: Amaç ("fire drill" parafrazı). A "fire" kelimesini gerçek yangın sanıyor; D "lawn" kelimesini yanlış kullanıyor.

questions.stem: What are residents told to do?
options: Take the elevators to the ground floor
Wait outside until staff say they can return
Stay in their rooms for fifteen minutes
Meet in the lobby of Hall B

why.en: Detail (paraphrase). A contradicts "do not use the elevators"; C misuses "fifteen minutes".
why.tr: Ayrıntı (parafraz). A "asansör kullanmayın" ile çelişiyor; C "on beş dakika" bilgisini yanlış kullanıyor.

options: The usual classroom is being repaired.
Dr. Morales asked for a larger screen.
Too many people signed up for the usual room.
The start time of the lecture changed.

questions.stem: What does the speaker recommend?
options: Registering online for a seat
Bringing a participation form
Sitting in the assigned section
Arriving before the talk begins

why.en: Detail (paraphrase of "arrive a few minutes early"). C contradicts "no assigned seating".
why.tr: Ayrıntı ("birkaç dakika erken gelin" parafrazı). C "numaralı oturma yok" bilgisiyle çelişiyor.

screen.title: Announcement: Gym closed on Saturday
screen.prompt: Listen to an announcement at the sports center.

audio.text: Hello, everyone. The gym will be closed this Saturday for its monthly cleaning. It will open again on Sunday at eight a.m. The swimming pool will stay open as usual on Saturday, and the changing rooms next to it can be used. Thank you.

options: The pool will be cleaned.
The gym will be closed.
The gym will open at eight.
A swimming class will start.

The deadline for submitting theses
The way theses are handed in
The number of copies every student prints

why.tr: Ana değişiklik ("e-posta yerine çevrim içi portal" parafrazı). A: kurallar değişmiyor, yalnızca kontrol ediliyor.

questions.stem: What is implied about students who wait until the last day to submit?
options: They will receive a lower grade for being late.
They will have to deliver two bound copies.
They will be allowed to send the thesis by email.
They may not have time to fix formatting problems.

why.en: Inference from "allow extra time for corrections". B applies only to architecture students.

audio.text: Didn't you say the study group was meeting in the library today?

Yes, the library closes at nine tonight.

audio.text: Where can I pick up my student ID card?

You'll need a recent photo for that.
It stays valid for four years.

audio.text: How long does the shuttle take to get downtown?

options: About twenty minutes, if traffic is light.
It leaves every half hour from here.
Downtown is really crowded today.
I usually ride my bike there.

why.en: A "how long" question. B gives a frequency (a classic trap).
why.tr: Süre sorusu. B sıklık veriyor (ETS'nin klasik tuzağı).

audio.text: I'm sorry, I can't make it to your presentation tomorrow.

options: No problem, I'll send you the slides.
It starts at ten in room two-oh-four.
I made it all myself, actually.
Tomorrow works better for me too.

why.en: Responding to an apology. C repeats "make it" with a different meaning.
why.tr: Özre karşılık. C "make it" ifadesini yanlış anlamda tekrar ediyor.

audio.text: Would you mind opening the window? It's really warm in here.

options: Sure, let me get that for you.
I don't mind warm weather at all.
The window looks out on the garden.
It was even warmer yesterday.

why.tr: Rica → kabul. B "mind" ve "warm" kelimelerini tekrar edip isteği yanıtlamıyor.

audio.text: Have you decided which elective to take next term?

options: I'm leaning toward the photography course.
Yes, I decided to take the bus instead.
Next term starts in early September.
The electives are all listed online.

why.en: "Which class" → a choice. D is true but is not an answer.
why.tr: Hangi ders → seçim. D doğru bir bilgi ama yanıt değil.

audio.text: The printer on this floor is out of paper again.

options: There's a box in the supply closet.
I printed my essay last night.
This floor is the quietest one.
Paper is cheaper if you buy it online.

why.en: Problem → solution. B repeats the word "printed".
why.tr: Sorun → çözüm. B "printed" ile kelime tekrarı.

audio.text: Why did the professor cancel today's lecture?

options: She's at a conference in Chicago.
The lecture is in the main hall.
Yes, she cancelled it this morning.
I'll take notes for you next time.

audio.text: Can I borrow your calculator for the exam?

options: Sorry, I need it myself.
The exam is on Friday morning.
It's a scientific calculator.
I borrowed it from the library.

why.tr: Rica → ret gerekçesiyle. D "borrow" kelimesini tekrar ediyor.

audio.text: What time does the cafeteria close?

options: At eight on weekdays.
I had pasta for lunch.
Yes, it's very close to here.
The food there is great.

audio.text: Is this seat taken?

The seats are all blue.
It's a long class.

Yes, the study is on the left.
Tonight is really cold.
I want a new notebook.

audio.text: Where did you buy that backpack?

options: At the campus store.
It's very heavy.
I bought it last year.
Yes, it's new.

It's on Monday.
I really like math.
Yes, I took it.

The boxes are brown.
I carried them yesterday.

The course starts next week.

The books cost more than I expected.

It holds about ten thousand people.

I borrowed a book.

On the table.

At the stadium.
I like soccer.

audio.text: Today let's look at how bats find their way in complete darkness. Most bats rely on a process called echolocation. screen.title: Academic Talk: The rise of linear perspective
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an art history class.

audio.text: Let's turn to one of the great technical advances of the Renaissance: linear perspective. Before the fifteenth century, European painters certainly suggested depth. They placed distant figures higher in the picture or made them smaller, but they lacked a consistent system, and different objects in the same painting often seemed to recede at different angles.

In Florence, early in the fifteenth century, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi carried out a famous demonstration. He painted a small panel showing the city's baptistery and drilled a hole through it. A viewer looked through the hole from the back while holding a mirror in front of the panel, so the reflected painting could be compared directly with the real building. The two lined up remarkably well.

The principle behind this is that parallel lines moving away from the viewer appear to meet at a single point, which we now call the vanishing point. In the 1430s, Leon Battista Alberti described the method in writing, which allowed it to spread far beyond Brunelleschi's circle. Keep in mind, though, that perspective wasn't only about accuracy. Painters used the vanishing point to guide the viewer's eye, often toward the most important figure in the scene.

screen.title: Academic Talk: Path dependence
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an economics class.

audio.text: Let's talk about a concept economists call path dependence. The basic idea is that decisions made in the past can limit the choices available today, even when the original reasons no longer apply.

The classic example is the keyboard layout most of you are using right now, known as QWERTY. It was designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters. One popular explanation is that it placed common letter pairs apart so the metal arms wouldn't jam, although historians still argue about how much that really mattered. Either way, the jamming problem disappeared long ago. Other layouts have been designed since then. The Dvorak keyboard, for example, put the most common letters on the middle row, where your fingers already rest, and some people claim it's faster. Yet QWERTY is everywhere.

Why? Because once millions of people had learned it, and schools taught it, and manufacturers produced it, switching became very costly. A new layout would have to be better by enough to make everyone relearn typing at the same time. So the old standard survives, not necessarily because it's the best, but because everyone else is already using it. And economists find the same pattern whenever the value of a choice depends on what everyone else has already chosen.

screen.title: Academic Talk: Managing shared resources
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an economics class.

audio.text: In economics there's a well-known idea called the tragedy of the commons. Picture a pasture that everyone in a village may use. Each herder reasons that adding one more cow brings him the full benefit of that cow, while the cost, slightly less grass, is shared by everyone. So each herder adds cows, and eventually the pasture is ruined, even though no one wanted that outcome.

For a long time, economists assumed there were only two solutions: either the government controls the resource, or it's divided into private property. But the political economist Elinor Ostrom challenged that view. She studied fisheries, forests, and irrigation systems around the world that communities had managed successfully for centuries without either solution.

What did those communities have in common? Ostrom found that they set clear boundaries around who could use the resource, they made their own rules about how much each person could take, and, this is important, they monitored one another and applied gradually increasing penalties to people who broke the rules. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in economics, partly for this work. So the lesson isn't that shared resources are always doomed. It's that the outcome depends on how the users organize themselves.

screen.title: Academic Talk: The serial position effect
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a talk in a psychology class.

audio.text: Today I want to talk about something you've probably experienced without realizing it. Imagine I read you a list of twenty words and then ask you to write down as many as you can remember. Most people recall the first few words and the last few words quite well, but the words in the middle tend to disappear. Psychologists call this the serial position effect.

So why does it happen? The words at the beginning get more rehearsal. When you hear the first word, you repeat it to yourself a few times, and that repetition helps move it into long-term memory. By the time the middle of the list arrives, you're trying to rehearse many words at once, so each one gets less attention. The words at the end are a different story. They're still sitting in short-term memory when you start writing, so you can simply read them off, so to speak.

Here's the interesting part. If I make you wait thirty seconds and count backward before you write, the advantage for the final words disappears, but the advantage for the first words remains. That tells us two different memory systems are involved. So, practically speaking, when you study, try not to always start from the same page. Otherwise the middle chapters will always get the least attention.

screen.title: Academic Talk: The wolves of Yellowstone
screen.prompt: Listen to part of a lecture in an environmental science class.

audio.text: In 1995, wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park after an absence of about seventy years. What happened next became one of the most famous stories in ecology. Without wolves, elk had grazed freely along the rivers, eating young willow and aspen trees before they could grow. Once wolves returned, the story goes, elk began avoiding open river valleys where they could easily be hunted. The trees recovered, beavers returned to use the wood, and their dams created ponds that supported fish and birds. Ecologists call a chain of effects like this a trophic cascade.

Now, it's a great story, and parts of it are clearly true. But more recent research suggests the picture is messier. Elk numbers also fell because of hunting by people, harsh winters, and a growing population of bears. And in some areas the willows haven't recovered at all, because without beaver dams the water table had dropped too low for the trees to grow back. In other words, removing a predator can trigger changes that simply adding it back doesn't reverse.
So what's the lesson? Not that the wolves didn't matter. They did. The lesson is that ecosystems don't always work like a light switch. Restoring one species is often only the first step.

screen.title: Color Words and Perception
screen.directions: Read an Academic Passage — upper module
text: Languages differ considerably in how they divide the color spectrum. Russian, for instance, obligatorily distinguishes between lighter blues (goluboy) and darker blues (siniy), whereas English speakers use a single basic term. This raises a question that has long intrigued linguists and psychologists: does the vocabulary a person habitually uses shape the way that person actually perceives the world?

Experimental evidence suggests a modest but measurable influence. In one study, Russian speakers distinguished between two shades of blue more rapidly when the shades straddled the boundary between goluboy and siniy than when both fell within a single category; English speakers showed no comparable advantage. Crucially, the effect vanished when participants simultaneously performed a verbal task that occupied their linguistic resources.

Researchers therefore caution against strong claims. Language does not appear to determine what people are capable of seeing; it seems instead to provide a convenient shortcut that accelerates certain judgments whenever linguistic processing is available.

screen.title: Underground Fungal Networks
screen.directions: Read an Academic Passage — upper module
text: Beneath most forests lies an extensive web of fungal threads known as mycorrhizal networks. These fungi colonize the roots of trees, supplying them with water and mineral nutrients such as phosphorus in exchange for sugars that the trees produce through photosynthesis.

Because a single network can connect the roots of many different trees, researchers have proposed that carbon and other resources may travel from one tree to another through these shared connections. Some experiments have reported that seedlings growing in deep shade receive carbon from larger neighbors, which might improve their chances of survival.

Nevertheless, the more dramatic claims, for instance that mature trees deliberately nurture their offspring or warn neighbors of insect attacks, remain contested. Critics note that many field studies were small, that the direction of transfer is difficult to measure, and that fungi may move resources primarily for their own benefit rather than for that of the forest.

text: Until the late nineteenth century, most towns set their clocks by the sun. Noon was the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky, so the time in one city could differ by several minutes from the time in a city a short distance to the east or west.

screen.title: Urban Heat Islands
text: On a summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Scientists call this an urban heat island. The main cause is the material that cities are built from: asphalt, concrete and brick absorb sunlight during the day and slowly release that heat at night.

For this reason, staying up all night before an exam may actually harm performance.

text: Main Library — new loan policy

Effective March 1, the main library will replace its fixed loan periods with a demand-based system. Items with no waiting list will renew automatically up to five times, so most borrowers will no longer need to visit the desk. However, once another user places a hold on an item you have borrowed, your loan will be shortened to seven days, and you will receive an email with the new due date. Overdue fines are being abolished; instead, borrowing privileges will be suspended until held items are returned. Laptops and other equipment remain excluded from the new system.

options: How long people keep items will depend on whether others want them
Borrowers must now renew every item at the front desk
The library will begin charging higher fines for late returns
Laptops may now be borrowed for longer periods

why.en: Main change (paraphrase): the loan period depends on demand. B and C contradict the text; D is equipment that is excluded.
why.tr: Ana değişiklik (parafraz): süre talebe bağlı. B ve C metnin tersi; D hariç tutulan ekipman.

text: Revised Overnight Parking Policy

why.tr: Ana değişiklik (parafraz). A aşırı genelleme (gündüz hâlâ park edebilirler); C son cümleyle çelişiyor.

From: Daniel Reyes (Apartment 4B)

Subject: Water shut-off on Thursday

Hi everyone, the building manager asked me to pass this on.
